query: Which material can be used for Temperature-dependent plastic deformation behaviors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) will exhibit superior temperature‐dependent plastic deformation behavior compared to conventional FCC alloys by activating different deformation mechanisms as the temperature changes.
generation.material_initial_state: As-prepared, homogenized, single-phase equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA with an FCC structure and a uniformly distributed random lattice of constituent atoms.
generation.intervention: Apply mechanical loading (e.g., tensile or compression tests) over a wide temperature range (from cryogenic temperatures ~77 K to elevated temperatures up to 800–1000 K).
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under controlled strain rates in an environment with systematically varied temperatures, ensuring maintenance of the alloy's phase stability.
generation.structural_mediator: The intrinsic random lattice distortions and the large number of slip systems inherent to the equiatomic FCC HEA structure mediate the transition among different deformation mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, deformation is mainly accommodated by partial dislocation nucleation (including stacking faults and twinning) leading to superplastic-like reorientation phenomena, whereas at higher temperatures, increased dislocation mobility and grain boundary sliding contribute to maintaining strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy is predicted to show improved yield strength and ductility over a wide temperature range with observable transitions from dislocation-mediated hardening and twinning at low temperatures to thermally activated mechanisms at high temperatures. This enhanced temperature-dependent plasticity should outperform conventional FCC alloys under equivalent testing conditions.
generation.baseline: Compared to standard single-phase FCC alloys and single-component nanowires (e.g., Ag nanowires), the CoCrFeMnNi HEA is expected to maintain a more favorable balance between strength and ductility across the considered temperature range.
generation.boundary: The predicted superior mechanical performance is contingent upon the HEA retaining a stable single-phase structure; deviations such as phase segregations or significant microstructural changes at extreme temperatures or under very high strain rates might mitigate the observed benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative thresholds for the transition between dislocation-dominated and grain-boundary influenced deformation, as well as the relative contributions of each mechanism at different temperatures, remain to be precisely defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples under identical processing conditions to ensure a homogeneous, single-phase state. Subject them to uniaxial tensile tests at temperatures ranging from 77 K to 1000 K with controlled strain rates. Concurrently test a conventional single-phase FCC alloy as a control. Measure stress–strain responses, yield strengths, ductility, and specific deformation features (e.g., twinning, dislocation patterns) using in situ microscopy and post-mortem analysis.
measurements: Yield strength and ductility (elongation to failure)
Microstructural characterization (via TEM/SEM) to assess dislocation behavior, twinning, and phase stability
Grain size and possible phase segregation analysis by X-ray diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CoCrFeMnNi HEA does not maintain or exceed the mechanical performance (e.g., yield strength and ductility) observed in the conventional FCC alloy over the test temperature range, or if no clear transition in deformation mechanisms can be observed, then the hypothesis that its unique structure leads to superior temperature-dependent plasticity would be falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
